title: Glistening Spiral Galaxy
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2541, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA Acknowledgments: PI: M T. Patterson (New Mexico State University) Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), Mahdi Zamani & Davide de Martin

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Spiral arms wind around NGC 2541 in fine detail in this image from Kitt Peak National Observatory's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope. It is classified as an unbarred spiral galaxy, with sweeping spiral arms but none of the central bar-shaped structure seen in galaxies such as the Milky Way.

At a distance of 37 million light-years, NGC 2541 sits in Lynx, a constellation squeezed in among Ursa Major, Gemini and Leo. Lynx was one of 10 constellations newly introduced in the 17th century by the astronomer Johannes Hevelius.

Because its stars are so dim, Hevelius said that only the lynx-eyed, meaning people with unusually sharp vision, could ever find it. Astronomers sort galaxies into a variety of types, and whether a spiral has a central bar is one of the features they use to classify it.
scale: NGC 2541 lies 37 million light-years from Earth, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: Taken with the Mosaic camera on the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope through U, B, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
